steps.prompt: Five friends earn $10$, $12$, $12$, $15$ and $200$ dollars a week. What is a "typical" amount? Would you use the mean or the median?

cards.title: Centre and spread
cards.body: Mean $=$ sum $\div$ count. The median is the middle value in order (the mean of the two middle ones when the count is even). Range $=$ largest $-$ smallest. Standard deviation measures how spread out the data is around the mean: bunched data has a smaller one.

cards.title: Worked example: an outlier
cards.problem: Five friends earn $10$, $12$, $12$, $15$ and $200$ dollars a week. Find the mean and the median.

steps.text: In order, the median is the third value.
The $200$ pulls the mean far up, but the median barely moves: here the median is the better "typical" value.

cards.title: Worked example: a missing value
cards.problem: The mean of $4$ test scores is $82$. What score on a fifth test makes the mean $85$?

steps.text: Turn each mean into a total. The four scores total $4 \times 82 = 328$.
The fifth score is the difference.

cards.title: Samples and conclusions
cards.body: A random sample lets you generalise to the population it was chosen from, with a margin of error; a bigger sample gives a smaller margin of error. Only a randomised experiment shows cause and effect. In an observational study a link (correlation) does not prove that one thing causes the other.

prompts: Describe a situation where the median tells you more than the mean.
